newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS - ABARE sees rise in Australian coal exports.
newsitem.headline: RTRS - ABARE sees rise in Australian coal exports.

text.p: Australia's coal export earnings are forecast to rise six percent in 1996/97 mainly due to increased demand for thermal coal, the Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) said.
In its September quarter Commodities bulletin, ABARE forecast export earnings of A$8.241 billion in the year to June 30 1997 up from an estimated A$7.756 billion in 1995/96.
Thermal coal exports were expected to jump 15 percent in 1996/97 to 70.4 million tonnes, more than making up for a forecast 4.1 percent fall in prices to A$47.3 per tonne.

In contrast, a relatively tight world market for metallurgical coal was expected to raise prices by 2.8 percent to A$63.0 per tonne in 1996/97, while export volumes were seen rising only modestly to 78.0 million tonnes from 77.3 million.
"Growth in Australia's coking coal exports depends on a range of technology issues, but most importantly on increasing blast furnace steel production," ABARE said.

"Strong steel demand, particularly in Asia, and increased steel production in South Korea, Taiwan and India are expected to provide most of the impetus for increased coking coal demand," the government agency said.
Australia's total coal production was seen rising 4.6 percent to 205.3 million tonnes in 1996/97 from a downward revised estimate of 196.3 million in 1995/96.

ABARE said continued substitution toward lower quality coking coals and the increased use of pulverised coal injection in Japan were expected to continue the gradual erosion of Japan's dominant position in the coking coal market.

Countries with expanding steel production such as India, Taiwan and South Korea were becoming increasingly important and was expected to affect the bargaining position of Japan's steel mills, ABARE said.
India would be a key nation in coking coal markets of the future, said ABARE, predicting a nine percent rise in Indian consumption of Australian coking coal to 10.8 million tonnes in 1996/97.
ABARE saw strengthening demand for thermal coal, in 1996/97, particularly in Asia, where Japan, India and China were all seen increasing their consumption.
However, an expansion in world thermal coal production meant the outlook for prices remained subdued, it said.
